author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The confidence which the Directory has shown me under all circumstances renders it my duty to inform them of all my actions. […]”

context: Paris. To Le Tourneur: The confidence which the Directory has shown me under all circumstances renders it my duty to inform them of all my actions.
voice: The confidence which the Directory has shown me under all circumstances renders it my duty to inform them of all my actions
tweet: I have asked Barras to tell the Directory of my marriage to Citoyenne Tascher Beauharnais. It binds me closer to the country — a pledge that I seek salvation in the Republic alone.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-chief Bonaparte reviewed the looth demi-brigade, &c. He is satisfied with the appearance of the troops, their sentiments of devotion towards the Republic, and their resolution to conquer. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To the Directory: I have been for several days in the midst of the army.
tweet: I have taken command. The administration is bad but not hopeless — I threaten the thieving contractors, then flatter them, and the army gets bread, meat and arrears. Tell the Directors their orders will be carried out; I march shortly.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I had Barras inform the Directory of my marriage to Citoyenne Tascher Beauharnais. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Barras told: married to Citoyenne Tascher Beauharnais. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.

tweet: I had Barras inform the Directory of my marriage to Citoyenne Tascher Beauharnais. The union is sealed; Josephine is now my wife.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter received. I dined today with General Schérer and your wife. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Dined with Schérer and your wife; glad to oblige her. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu votre lettre. J'ai diné aujourd'hui chez le général Schérer avec votre femme.
tweet: Your letter received. I dined today with General Schérer and your wife. Social ties bind the officer corps as much as duty.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Soldiers, you are naked, ill-fed; the Government owes you much and can give you nothing. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Nus, mal nourris: the most famous proclamation of the age. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Soldats, vous êtes nus, mal nourris; le Gouvernement vous doit beaucoup, il ne peut rien vous donner.
tweet: Soldiers, you are naked, ill-fed; the government owes you much and can give you nothing. But I will lead you to the most fertile plains in the world. There you will find honour, glory, and wealth.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Enclosed the cavalry movement state; regiments arrive daily. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Cavalry movement states; regiments arriving daily. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous trouverez ci-joint l'état du mouvement de la cavalerie; vous y verrez qu'il arrive des régiments.
tweet: Enclosed the cavalry movement state; regiments arrive daily. The horse is the eye of the army; I will not be blind.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall be charmed to be of service to her It is said that the Genoese offer us 3,000,000 francs. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To Faypoult: Genoa to pay three millions.
voice: I shall be charmed to be of service to her It is said that the Genoese offer us 3,000,000 francs
tweet: Your letter is here — I dined with Schérer and your wife yesterday, and I shall gladly serve her. Take the Genoese 3,000,000 francs quietly, and keep their friendship; their enmity would ruin our trade and my campaign.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Warmly received by the army, whose confidence obliges my liveliest gratitude. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Well received by the army; Schérer pure and enlightened. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai été très-bien reçu par l'armée, qui me montre une confiance qui m'oblige à une vive reconnaissance.
tweet: Warmly received by the army, whose confidence obliges my liveliest gratitude. I will not betray the trust of men who follow me into fire.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The 209th's 3rd battalion stands guilty of disobedience and mutiny. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: 209th refuses to march: disobedience and mutiny. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le 3e bataillon de la 209e demi-brigade s'est rendu coupable de désobéissance et d'esprit de mutinerie.
tweet: The 209th third battalion stands guilty of disobedience and mutiny. Discipline is the soul of armies; without it we are a mob. The ringleaders will answer for this.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The cavalry divides in two divisions. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Cavalry in two divisions: hussars, chasseurs assigned. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: La cavalerie sera partagée en deux divisions.
tweet: The cavalry divides in two divisions. I am arranging the horse for maximum effect on the coming march.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Parra will at once requisition Antibes' administrators. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Antibes communes to furnish momentary supplies. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général de brigade Parra de requérir sur-le-champ les corps administratifs de cette commune.
tweet: I general parra will at once requisition antibes administrators. Supply must flow without delay.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief reviewed the 100th and 165th demi-brigades. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Reviewed 100th, 165th and Montfernie battalion. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef a passé la revue de la 100e demi-brigade et de la 165e.
tweet: The General-in-Chief reviewed the 100th and 165th demi-brigades. Their bearing pleases me; they will do their duty.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tonight deliver the staff officers' roll marching on the 12th. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Tonight: staff, artillery and engineers lists for the 12th. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous me remettrez ce soir l'état nominatif des officiers de l'état-major qui partent le 12.
tweet: I want the staff roll tonight of every officer marching. The command must be complete before we move.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Adjutant-General Chabran leaves Nice today for Albenga post-haste. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Chabran to Albenga post-haste, 11 Germinal. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné à l'adjudant général Chabran de partir de Nice aujourd'hui pour se rendre le plus promptement à Albenga.
tweet: I adjutant-general chabran leaves Nice today for Albenga post-haste. Speed in transmission is everything.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “One for 172,800 francs, drawn on Cadiz, has just been returned, which augments our difficulties. *' I found this army not only destitute of everything, but without discipline and in a chronic state of insubordination. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

voice: I found this army not only destitute of everything, but without discipline and in a chronic state of insubordination
tweet: Enclosed: General Colli letter with my answer, which I hope suits you. The treasury bills bounce — one for 172,800 francs drawn on Cadiz just came back. I found this army destitute and mutinous, singing for the Dauphin; two officers face court martial.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will find the details of the battles of Montenotte and Millesimo in the report forwarded to the Directory. I cannot conceal from you that I am seconded neither by the artillery nor the engineers, as, in spite of your orders, I have not a single one of the officers I asked for. […]”

context: Carcare. To Director Carnot: You will find the details of the battles of Montenotte and Millesimo in the report forwarded to the Directory.
voice: @carnot You will find the details of the battles of Montenotte and Millesimo in the report forwarded to the Directory
tweet: Montenotte and Millesimo are in my report — but I am seconded by neither guns nor engineers; despite your orders I have not one officer I asked for. I took Montezemolo myself and must survey Ceva in person while Beaulieu rages.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have 100,000 men against me, and can oppose only 34,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry to that force. The enemy possesses strong places and a numerous and efficient artillery […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Carru. To the Directory: I have 100,000 men against me, and can oppose only 34,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry to that force.
voice: I have 100,000 men against me, and can oppose only 34,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry to that force
tweet: Mondovi does the troops the greatest honour. But you have no idea of this army state — undermined, breadless, undisciplined when I came. I work all night, I make examples; the breadless soldier shames us all. The enemy is strong and fights well.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have learned with pain that our troops allowed themselves to be surprised yesterday at the village of St. Michel. […] You must not be astonished, my dear general, at the little check you have received; it will only be the prelude to our victory. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Eve of Montenotte: a check at San Michele, answered with a promise of revenge. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: I have learned with pain that our troops allowed themselves to be surprised yesterday at the village of St. Michel. By these various movements you will be in a pOSITION to take your revenge in a brilliant fashion.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Michel By these various movements you will be in a position to take your revenge in a brilliant fashion You must not be astonished, my dear general, at the little check you have received; it will only be the prelude to our victory. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To General Serurier: Michel By these various movements you will be in a position to take your revenge in a brilliant fashion You must not be astonished, my dear general…
voice: @serurier Michel By these various movements you will be in a position to take your revenge in a brilliant fashion You must not be astonished, my dear general, at the little check you have received
tweet: It pained me to hear our troops surprised at St. Michel. But these movements put you in place for a brilliant revenge — this little check is only the prelude to our victory.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief renews orders to hasten the new organisation. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Hasten the new organisation work in every division. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef renouvelle l'ordre d'accélérer le travail relatif à la nouvelle organisation.
tweet: The General-in-Chief renews orders to hasten the new organisation. Disorder is the enemy of victory; I will have order.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A 400-sack contribution levied on Oneille valley. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: 400 sacks on Oneille valley, 200 on the district. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef ordonne une contribution de quatre cents sacs dans la vallée d'Oneille.
tweet: I a 400-sack contribution levied on oneille valley. The army feeds itself from the land it conquers.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Convene a Nice military commission for émigré Moulin, taken at Ormea. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Émigré Moulin to military commission at Nice. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous voudrez bien faire réunir une commission militaire à Nice pour y juger l'émigré Moulin, pris à Ormea.
tweet: I convene a Nice military commission for émigré moulin, taken at Ormea. Traitors face military justice.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have transferred my head-quarters to Albenga. The movement which I found commenced against Genoa has drawn the enemy out of his winter quarters. Beaulieu has published a manifesto, to which I shall reply after the battle. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Headquarters moved up; Genoa's alarm spoiled his plan to catch Beaulieu napping. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: I have transferred my head-quarters to Albenga. The movement against Genoa drew the enemy from winter quarters. Beaulieu published a manifesto; I shall reply after the battle.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Distress has authorised insubordination, and without discipline victory is out of the question. I hope all this will be changed in the course of a few days. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Albenga. To the Directory: Distress has authorised insubordination, and without discipline victory is out of the question.
voice: I hope all this will be changed in the course of a few days
tweet: I have moved headquarters to Albenga. The stir against Genoa annoys me — it forces that Republic hostile, wakes the enemy I meant to catch napping, and will cost us men. Colli sent an envoy under truce; I arrested him and ordered court martial — nothing shields a parricide.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Raise a Laigueglia–Pietra brigade for carts, forage, hospitals. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Mule brigades Laigueglia–Pietra for forage and hospitals. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous donnerez les ordres pour qu'il soit levé, pour les charrois, fourrages et hôpitaux, une brigade de Laigueglia à Pietra.
tweet: I raise a laigueglia-pietra brigade for carts, forage, hospitals. Logistics win campaigns.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Reviewed the 39th and 69th with published satisfaction. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: 39th and 69th reviewed with published satisfaction. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef a passé la revue des 39e et 69e demi-brigades, avec satisfaction publiée par la voie de l'ordre.
tweet: I reviewed the and with published satisfaction. Good troops deserve recognition.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Levy two hundred mules at Pieve, Ormea and Garessio for food. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Two hundred mules at Pieve, Ormea, Garessio for food. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous donnerez l'ordre pour que l'on lève à Pieve, Ormea et Garessio, une division de deux cents mulets, pour les vivres.
tweet: I levy two hundred mules at pieve, Ormea and garessio for food. The army moves on its stomach.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, an émigré is a parricidal son no rank can sanctify; yours dishonour your army. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: An émigré is a parricidal son; his presence dishonours your army. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Monsieur, un émigré est un fils parricide qu'aucun caractère ne peut rendre sacré; ceux qui sont dans votre armée la déshonorent.
tweet: Sir, an émigré is a parricidal son no rank can sanctify; yours dishonour your army. I will not treat with traitors.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I learn Genoa molests patriots and troubles France's friends. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Genoa molests patriots while sheltering émigrés. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'apprends que le Gouvernement de Gênes moleste les patriotes et inquiète les amis de la France.
tweet: I learn Genoa molests patriots and troubles France's friends. The Republic protects its own wherever they are.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Hold your troops ready to march at first signal, food issued. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Troops ready to march at first signal, with food issued. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous donne l'ordre de tenir les troupes prêtes à marcher au premier signal, avec les vivres distribués.
tweet: Hold your troops ready to march at first signal, food issued; I want them ready.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Augereau marches two demi-brigades and four squadrons to Mallare. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Two demi-brigades and four squadrons to Mallare by shortest road. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Augereau partira avec ses deux demi-brigades et quatre escadrons pour Mallare par le plus court chemin.
tweet: I Augereau marches two demi-brigades and four squadrons to mallare. The offensive begins now.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Finale's artillery marches with 8-pounder, 4s, howitzer and all munitions. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: 8-pounder, two 4s, howitzer, two 3s: march with all munitions. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné à l'officier d'artillerie à Finale de partir avec la pièce de 8, deux pièces de 4, un obusier et toutes ses munitions.
tweet: I finale's artillery marches with 8-pounder, 4s, howitzer and all munitions. Guns follow the bayonet.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Italian campaign has commenced. I have forwarded a report on the battle of Montenotte. After manoeuvring for three days in order to conceal his intentions, Beaulieu attacked the right of our army with 10,000 men. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: First victory dispatch: Montenotte, three days of manoeuvre. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: The Italian campaign has commenced. I have forwarded a report on the battle of Montenotte. After manoeuvring three days to conceal his intentions, Beaulieu attacked the right of our army with 10,000 men.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will find the details of the battles of Montenotte and Millesimo in the report forwarded to the Directory. I cannot conceal from you that I am seconded neither by the artillery nor the engineers, as, in spite of your orders, I have not a single one of the officers I asked for. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content after Montenotte–Millesimo. Fighting Paris as well as Piedmont: no engineers, no artillery officers sent. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: You will find the details of the battles of Montenotte and Millesimo in the report forwarded to the Directory. I cannot conceal that I am seconded neither by the artillery nor the engineers, as, in spite of your orders, I have not a single one of the officers I asked for.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “An hour after noon he attacked the redoubt of Monte Legino, which was our last line of defence. The enemy returned several times to the charge, but the redoubt, defended by 1,500 men, was rendered impregnable by the courage of those who defended it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Carcare. To the Directory: The enemy returned several times to the charge, but the redoubt, defended by 1,500 men, was rendered impregnable by the courage of those who defended it.
voice: An hour after noon he attacked the redoubt of Monte Legino, which was our last line of defence
tweet: The campaign opens — my Montenotte report is enclosed. Beaulieu came with 10,000 men; Cervoni held with free soldiers courage. I saw his true aim at once, and ordered Cervoni to slip away by night march to my centre.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The soldier without bread is driven to commit acts which make one blush to be a man. […] I have 100,000 men against me, and can oppose only 34,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry to that force. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content after Mondovi. Mondovi report: the army he found — without bread, without discipline — and made examples. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: The soldier without bread is driven to commit acts which make one blush to be a man. I have 100,000 men against me, and can oppose only 34,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry to that force.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Everything is going on well. There is not so much pillaging. The first thirst of an army in want of everything has been quenched. There was an excuse for these unfortunate fellows who after having sighed for three years on the summit of the Alps, reached the promised land and desired to enjoy it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Pillage punished: three shot, hard labour. Order before politics. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: I everything is going on well. There is not so much pillaging. The first thirst of an army in want of everything has been quenched.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Destitute of everything, you have supplied everything. You have won battles without cannon, crossed rivers without bridges, made forced marches without shoes, bivouacked without brandy and often without bread. […] Friends, I promise you this conquest; but one condition you must swear to fulfil: respect the peoples you deliver. Else you will not be the liberators of peoples, but their scourge. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: The Cherasco proclamation, in French at last: destitute of everything, supplied everything. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Dénués de tout, vous avez suppléé à tout. Vous avez gagné des batailles sans canons, passé des rivières sans ponts, fait des marches forcées sans souliers, bivouaqué sans eau-de-vie et souvent sans pain. […] Amis, je vous la promets cette conquête; mais il est une condition qu'il faut que vous juriez de remplir: respecter les peuples que vous délivrez. Sans cela, vous ne seriez pas les libérateurs des peuples, vous en seriez les fléaux.
tweet: Destitute of everything, you have supplied everything. You have won battles without cannon, crossed rivers without bridges, made forced marches without shoes, bivouacked without brandy and often without bread.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In three days discipline will be severely established, and astonished Italy will admire the moderation of our army as it already admires its courage. This occasions me a great deal of pain, and makes me pass very unhappy moments. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To the Directory: In three days discipline will be severely established, and astonished Italy will admire the moderation of our army as it already admires its courage.
voice: In three days discipline will be severely established, and astonished Italy will admire the moderation of our army as it already admires its courage
tweet: The first thirst is quenched — less pillaging now. Three shot, more to hard labour, and church thieves die tomorrow. In three days this army will be disciplined, and Italy will admire our moderation as it admires our courage. It pains me deeply.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The village of Coni has been occupied by our troops. I feel sure that you will approve of the suspension of arms granted to the Sardinians; it is an armistice accorded to one wing of an army, giving me time to beat the other. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Sardinia's armistice — signed against the Directory's orders: a king at his discretion. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: Coni is ours. I trust you approve my Sardinian armistice: truce with one wing while I beat the other. Their king yields three fortresses and half his realm. I cross the Adige for Germany by the Tyrol. My columns march; Beaulieu flees, but I shall catch him and tax Parma millions.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We reached Acqui yesterday. Beaulieu flies so fast that we cannot catch him Send me a geographical, historical, political, and topographical note on the imperial fiefs in the neighbourhood of Genoa; also a note on the Dukes of Parma, Placentia, and Modena; the forces they have in the field; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Connoisseur's shopping list: notes on fiefs, dukes — and their pictures and statues. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: We reached Acqui yesterday, but Beaulieu flies too fast to catch. Send me notes on everything around Genoa — the imperial fiefs, and the Dukes of Parma, Piacenza and Modena with the forces each has in the field.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your answer. I beg you will express to the Corps Legislatif the thanks of the army for the honourable decree which it has voted; it is the most grateful recompense that the army can receive. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Thanks of the army voted; devotion to the constitution professed — for now. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: I have your answer. Convey the army thanks to the Corps Législatif for its decree — no recompense touches soldiers more. As for me, my devotion to the constitution has never wavered; I saw it born amid passions trying to destroy the Republic.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The army of Italy is in the greatest distress It is every day reinforcedy and its necessities increase in proportion. When the Directory gave me the command of this army it drew up a plan of offensive warfare necessitating prompt measures and extraordinary resources. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: An army in distress: pay months late, needs growing with every recruit. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: My army of Italy is in the greatest distress. Every day brings recruits I cannot feed, while the Directory plan demands offensive warfare with prompt measures and extraordinary resources — yet even two sous to the men and eight francs to the officers goes unpaid.

tweet: Fortune frowns for the moment — no time for details. Lonato is won and my measures are vigorous; I have raised the Mantua siege with nearly all my forces. I have ridden five horses to death and cannot write the Directory.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

originalText: Il est ordonné au général Gaultier de partir sur-le-champ de Bozzolo pour se rendre à Castenedolo.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: I joubert at castiglione delle stiviere by six o'clock. Precision in timing wins battles.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

voice: In entering a public career I adopted for principle, Everything for the country 1
tweet: My brother the war commissary has run to Paris without leave, meddling in politics as always — order him to some army. Young Louis deserves your favor — he served me at Lonato.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My first thought is to write to you. Your health and your image have not been out of my mind for one moment during the whole way. I shall not be happy until I have received letters from you. I wait for them with impatience. It is not possible that you can realize my distress. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Brescia: first thought on arrival is her. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Vaubois note: Masséna reached Ala; tomorrow 8 or 9 a.m. she marches. […]”

tweet: I Vaubois note: Massena reached ala; tomorrow 8 or 9 a.m. She marches. The offensive continues.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If Naples is wanted, Citizen Directors, seriously consider reinforcements. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)

tweet: If Naples is wanted, Citizen Directors, seriously consider reinforcements. I cannot take Naples with what I have.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Masséna marches with all, artillery and 100 dragoons. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)

originalText: Il est ordonné au général Masséna de partir avec toute sa division, son artillerie et les 100 hommes du 15e dragons.
tweet: I Massena marches with all, artillery and 100 dragoons. The whole force moves as one.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Milan sends all disposable cavalry to Peschiera at once. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: All Milan disposable cavalry to Peschiera at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général commandant à Milan fera partir au plus tôt pour Peschiera tout ce qui se trouve à Milan de disponible en cavalerie.
tweet: I Milan sends all disposable cavalry to peschiera at once. The horse goes where the fight is.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Masséna marches tomorrow 22nd at 2 a.m. in greatest order. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Masséna marches at 2 a.m. in greatest order. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef ordonne au général Masséna de partir, demain 22, à deux heures du matin, dans le plus grand ordre.
tweet: I Massena marches tomorrow at 2 a.m. In greatest order. Night marches surprise the enemy.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Arrived here with all forces, chasing enemy posts. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 9:30 p.m.: arrived here with all forces, posts chased. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef me charge de vous prévenir que nous sommes arrivés ici, avec toutes nos forces, après en avoir chassé quelques postes.
tweet: I arrived here with all forces, chasing enemy posts. The pursuit is relentless.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “But should you ignore your own interests, and take up arms, we shall be terrible as the fire from heaven; we shall burn the houses and lay waste the territory of the villages which take part in a war that does not concern them. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Inhabitants Of The Tyrol, 1796-09-14

voice: @tyrol But should you ignore your own interests, and take up arms, we shall be terrible as the fire from heaven
tweet: Brave Tyrolians — I enter to force Vienna into a peace Europe needs, and your cause is mine. Your religion and customs are safe. But take arms against your own interests, and we shall be terrible as heaven fire — burned houses, wasted villages.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your character, sir, which all who know you praise, induces me to permit you to return to Ferrara and to throw the veil of oblivion over your conduct of last month. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To Cardinal Mattel: Your character, sir, which all who know you praise, induces me to permit you to return to Ferrara and to throw the veil of oblivion over your conduct of last month.
voice: @mattel Your character, sir, which all who know you praise, induces me to permit you to return to Ferrara and to throw the veil of oblivion over your conduct of last month
tweet: Your character, praised by all who know you, moves me to let you return to Ferrara, veiling last month in oblivion. You know the Testament too well for it to be more than forgetfulness — but priests in politics earn no respect. Return to your diocese.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “These two forces united make 53,000 men, and at present we have only 27,000; cavalry, gunners, sappers, drivers, etc., were also needed, and If the preservation of Italy be dear to you, Citizen Directors, send me all this aid […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To the Directory: These two forces united make 53,000 men, and at present we have only 27,000.
tweet: After St. George I tried to draw Wurmser out and weaken Mantua. I hold 18,900 watching and 9,000 besieging — but to winter in Italy I need 35,000 in the field and 18,000 at the siege: 53,000 against my 27,000. Send me everything.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “' I only wait for a favourable moment to fall upon Rome and to avenge the national honour. The chief object is to gain time The great art at present is to indulge in a little mutual recrimination in order to deceive that old fox. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To Cardinal Mattel: The chief object is to gain time The great art at present is to indulge in a little mutual recrimination in order to deceive that old fox.
voice: I only wait for a favourable moment to fall upon Rome and to avenge the national honour
tweet: Rome refuses peace, breaks the armistice, arms — she wants war and shall have it. But first one last effort: go to Rome, open the Pope eyes to his interests. He knows my strength; only my will stands between his temporal power and ruin.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Lombardy's people pronounce daily for us. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Lombardy pronounces daily; one great class waits to throw the glove. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le peuple de la Lombardie se prononce chaque jour davantage.
tweet: Lombardy pronounces for us daily.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Majesty, Europe desires peace; this disastrous war lasted too long. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Majesty, Europe desires peace; this disastrous war lasted too long. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Majesté, l'Europe veut la paix. Cette guerre désastreuse dure depuis trop longtemps.
tweet: Sire — all Europe desires peace, and I tell you plainly: this disastrous war has lasted too long.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They are all armed, and in some of the cantons the inhabitants are brave The King of Naples has raised a force of 60,000 men, and if he is to be attacked and dethroned that will require 18,000 infantry, and 3,000 cavalry Rome is strong owing to her fanaticism, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To the Directory: They are all armed, and in some of the cantons the inhabitants are brave The King of Naples has raised a force of 60,000 men…
tweet: Venice plots with Naples and the Pope while every Italian hates us. Naples has raised 60,000 men — dethroning him costs me 18,000 foot and 3,000 horse. Rome burns with fanaticism; if she declares, I guard my rear and hold her with 6,000 men.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think it would be well to except — first, the four deputies who took the crown to London; second, the six members composing the Council of State of the Viceroy, and lastly the emigres I have caused citizen Panatieri, Paoli's secretary, who came from London to intrigue, to be arrested at Leghorn. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To the Directory: Second, the six members composing the Council of State of the Viceroy, and lastly the emigres I have caused citizen Panatieri, Paoli's secretary…
voice: I think it would be well to except — first, the four deputies who took the crown to London
tweet: For the Corsican amnesty, except these men: the four deputies who carried the crown to London, the Viceroy's six councillors, and the émigrés. Panatieri — Paoli's secretary, come from London to intrigue — I have had arrested at Leghorn.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Patrol Verona–Bassano against French soldiers' excesses. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)

originalText: Vous donnerez ordre qu'il soit fait des patrouilles sur la route de Vérone à Bassano, pour arrêter les excès des militaires français.
tweet: I patrol Verona-bassano against French soldiers' excesses. Discipline protects the liberated.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Transfer all unserviceable wounded to Lyon. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Unserviceable wounded to Lyon under war minister's orders. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie d'ordonner que tous les blessés hors d'état de servir soient transférés à Lyon.
tweet: I Transfer all unserviceable wounded to Lyon. The hospitals must not choke on those who cannot fight.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Modena's armistice conditions stand unfulfilled. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Modena's unpaid contribution had last term the 4th Messidor. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les conditions de l'armistice conclu avec le duc de Modène n'ont pas été remplies.
tweet: Modena's armistice conditions stand unfulfilled. I hold them to their word.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The siege of Mantua, sir, is more disastrous for humanity than two campaigns. Brave men ought to affront danger, but not the pestilence of a marsh. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Chivalry to the enemy: Mantua's marshes kill more surely than battles. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: I tell you plainly, sir: the Mantua siege wastes humanity worse than two campaigns. Brave men should face danger, not marsh pestilence.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He compromised himself in '93 several times in spite of my reiterated advice. He wished to play the Jacobin. His sojourn at Marseilles would be dangerous for himself and the public weal as intriguers would get hold of him. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To Carnot: You have seen by the letter of my brother Lucien in what a state of exaltation he is.
tweet: You have seen Lucien exalted letter. He compromised himself repeatedly despite my warnings, playing Jacobin; Marseilles is dangerous for him and the public. Corsica is free — send him there, for his hot head cannot stay with the Rhine army.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Majesty, Europe desires peace. This disastrous war has lasted too long. I have the honour to notify to your Majesty that if you do not send plenipotentiaries to Paris to offer negotiations for peace, the Directory has ordered me to fill up the port of Trieste, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: A 27-year-old to an emperor: send plenipotentiaries — or lose Trieste. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: I write you plainly, Majesty: Europe cries for peace; this ruinous war outlasted itself.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have only too many honours, and my health is so impaired, that I think I shall be forced to demand a successor. I can no longer get on horseback; my courage alone remains, and that is not sufficient in a position like this. […]”
sourceTitle: To His Majesty The Emperor Of Germany, Milan, 1796-10-27
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To His Majesty The Emperor Of Germany: I have only too many honours, and my health is so impaired, that I think I shall be forced to demand a successor.
voice: I have only too many honours, and my health is so impaired, that I think I shall be forced to demand a successor
tweet: Sire — Europe desires peace; this disastrous war has lasted too long. Send plenipotentiaries to Paris, or I fill Trieste harbor and ruin your Adriatic houses. I have held back only to spare the innocent.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “For several days past we have been in observation along the Adige. Woe to him who miscalculates! ** We are now engaged in besieging Mantua. […]”
sourceTitle: To William Locker, Captain at Sea., 1796-11-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To William Locker: Woe to him who miscalculates! ** We are now engaged in besieging Mantua.
voice: We are now engaged in besieging Mantua
tweet: We are done with Corsica — greedy and jealous, its people are ruled only by shooting enemies and bribing friends. They already miss our silver.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “All this and the death of so many brave men " renders me circumspect; I no longer dare to expose myself as my death would discourage the troops and be a misfortune for those who are the object of all my care. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To the Directory: I no longer dare to expose myself as my death would discourage the troops and be a misfortune for those who are the object of all my care.
voice: I no longer dare to expose myself as my death would discourage the troops and be a misfortune for those who are the object of all my care
tweet: Vaubois panicked, losing 1,300 prisoners and guns, with a check at Caldiero — and so many brave dead make me circumspect. I no longer dare risk myself; my death would break the army. In a few days, one last effort.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Victual Verona citadel at once, 20 days for 600 men. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)

originalText: Faire approvisionner sur-le-champ la citadelle de Vérone, pour 20 jours et pour 600 hommes.
tweet: I Victual Verona citadel at once, 20 days for 600 men. The garrison must not starve.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter announcing the enemy's passage received. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Masséna reports the enemy passed: armies take note. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef vient de recevoir la lettre par laquelle vous annoncez que l'ennemi a passé.
tweet: Your letter announcing the enemy's passage received. I know they have crossed; I am ready.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Lombard legion's 1st cohort to Verona on the 15th, armed. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Lombard legion's 1st cohort to Verona on the 15th, armed. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: La 1re cohorte de la légion lombarde partira, le 15 du courant, avec armes et bagages, pour Vérone.
tweet: I lombard legion's cohort to Verona on the, armed. New troops join the line.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Southern sans-culottes: purge the Republic of tyrants. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Southern sans-culottes: purge the Republic of tyrants. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les sans-culottes du Midi ne doivent avoir d'autre sollicitude que de purger le territoire de la République des tyrans.
tweet: I southern sans-culottes: purge the Republic of tyrants. The Revolution spreads south.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The enemy crossed the Piave: hurry every depot forward. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Enemy crossed the Piave: hurry every depot and draft. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Nous sommes en présence de l'ennemi, qui a passé la Piave. Activez la marche de tous les dépôts.
tweet: I the enemy crossed the piave: hurry every depot forward. Supply lines must not be cut.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Mantua Nov. 6, lygd. " Soldiers: I am not satisfied with you; you have shown neither bravery, discipline, nor perseverance; no position could rally you; you abandoned yourselves to a panic-terror; you suffered yourselves to be driven from situations where a handful of brave men might have stopped an army. […]”
sourceTitle: Address During the Siege of Mantua, 1796-11-06
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Mantua besieged: address to the troops.
tweet: Soldiers, I am displeased: no courage, no discipline, no constancy. No ground rallied you; panic scattered you where a handful could have stood. I expect better of my army.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I arrived at Verona day before yesterday, my dearest love. Though fatigued I am very well; much prospered, and I love you always passionately. I mount my horse. I embrace you a thousand times. BONAPARTE.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Verona, day before yesterday arrived: fatigued, well, loving passionately. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).
tweet: I arrived at Verona day before yesterday, my dearest love. Though fatigued I am very well; much prospered, and I love you always passionately. I mount my horse. I embrace you a thousand times.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I do not love you at all; on the contrary, I detest you. You are a naughty woman, very crooked, very unfeeling, very ungenerous. Tu es une vilaine, bien gauche, bien bête, bien cendrillon. You do not write me at all. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: The famous scolding: 'I do not love you at all' — Arcole-eve jealousy. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).
tweet: I do not love you at all; on the contrary, I detest you. You are a naughty woman, very crooked, very unfeeling, very ungenerous. Tu es une vilaine, bien gauche, bien bete, bien cendrillon. You do not write me at all. My heart is torn by your silence.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Generals Verdier, Bon, Verne, and Lannes were all put hors de combat in the attempt. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To the Directory: Generals Verdier, Bon, Verne, and Lannes were all put hors de combat in the attempt.
tweet: Arcole has decided Italy, and I am spent with fatigue — I cannot recount the movements. The bridge was desperate: Verdier, Bon, Verne, Lannes all down in the attempt. When Augereau flag failed to move them, I went myself and asked: are you the conquerors of Lodi?

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I hope very soon, my sweet love, to be in your arms. I love you most passionately. […] All goes well. Wurmser was beaten yesterday under Mantua. There is nothing wanted by your husband but the love of Josephine, in order to be happy.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Wurmser beaten; loving 'à la fureur'. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).
tweet: I hope very soon, my sweet love, to be in your arms. I love you most passionately. All goes well. Wurmser was beaten yesterday under Mantua. There is nothing wanted by your husband but the love of Josephine, in order to be happy.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the express which Berthier had dispatched from Genoa. You had not time to write me. I feel it sensibly. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Milan, midnight: no letter — felt 'sensibly' amid gaiety. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).
tweet: I have received the express which Berthier had dispatched from Genoa. You had not time to write me. I feel it sensibly. Your letters are my life; without them I am incomplete.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The army of General Alvinzi is on the Brenta and in the Tyrol, and that of the Republic along the Adige Mantua is invested with the greatest care You will see by the Emperor's letter that Wurmser must be in extrernis The army returns which you have sent are full of errors The army of Italy, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Alvinzi on the Brenta; Wurmser in extremis; an army of 38,500 that should be 51,000. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: The army of General Alvinzi is on the Brenta and in the Tyrol, and that of the Republic along the Adige. Mantua is invested with the greatest care. You will see by the Emperor's letter that Wurmser must be in extremis. The army returns you sent are full of errors.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “This stratagem, worthy of my Lord Peterborough, had a great influence on the fortunes of the day. It is more than probable that in the following despatch Bonaparte, in accordance with custom, misrepresented numbers on both sides: […]”

context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To his chief of staff Berthier: This stratagem, worthy of my Lord Peterborough, had a great influence on the fortunes of the day.
tweet: Hercules rode round the Austrians with twenty-five trumpeters and blew such a blast as has not sounded since Jericho. That stratagem decided the day — and I made him captain, with seventy-two francs to each guide.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “And we are on the eve of an affair with the debris of all these armies, reinforced by 4,000 volunteers from Vienna, 3,000 men from the Rhine, 3,000 recruits who have already arrived, and 1,500 expected in January. BONAPARTE S POSITION. I 23 " It required good luck, and good play, to beat Alvinzi. […]”

context: Montenotte to Arcole: six victories, 15,000 prisoners, a legend made. To the Directory: The army of General Alvinzi is on the Brenta and in the Tyrol, and that of the Republic along the Adige Mantua is invested with the greatest care You will see by the…
tweet: Your returns are full of errors. Italy proper had 38,500 foot, plus 10,000 — 51,100 without losses. Deduct 4,000 killed, wounded unfit, 2,000 dead in hospital: 7,000 gone. Only 12,500 reinforcements in a campaign of so many battles.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marshal Berwick had the intendant of his army hung because provisions failed; and in the midst of abundance, and when paying five times more than is necessary, we are often in want. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Milan. To the Directory: Marshal Berwick had the intendant of his army hung because provisions failed.
tweet: Theft, not war, bleeds this army. The controller swindles, his clerks are incapable, everything is sold — we consume five times needful on false orders shared with contractors, while generals keep actresses. Laws fail; only a special court will do.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is this infamous conduct which has compromised our operations and caused the loss of a great number of our comrades. I consequently demand that these three men be condemned to death in order to alarm their accomplices, who are only too numerous in the army of Italy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

tweet: Bring Bockty, Chevilly and Descrivains before my court-martial — they robbed and endangered the army, and comrades died for it. I demand death, to terrify their many accomplices.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Brune received seven bullets in his uniform without being wounded, which was good luck. " Bonaparte.** Alvinzi, acting on the orders of the Aulic council, had suddenly attacked the French at several points. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Verona. To his war minister Clarke: Alvinzi, acting on the orders of the Aulic council, had suddenly attacked the French at several points.
tweet: I had barely left Roverbella when Verona was attacked — Massena plans took 600 prisoners and three guns, and Brune caught seven bullets without a scratch. Alvinzi strikes everywhere at once to blind me about Mantua.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will THE AULIC COUNCIL. I 29 march to Castelnovo and shoot the chief of the rebels, and send twenty hostages to Milan; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To General Rusca: Some unfortunate people have allowed themselves to be seduced by perfidious agents, who excite them to revolt and draw down upon them the horrors of war.
tweet: I will not suffer seduction and revolt to bring war horrors. Advance on Castelnovo, shoot the rebel chief, send twenty hostages to Milan. Raze the confessor house and raise a pyramid there: punishment of a priest who preached revolt and murder.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have caused these letters to be printed in the Bologna gazettes, so as to convince all Italy of the idiotic doting of these old cardinals. To-morrow I shall pass the Po, near Ferrara, and march on Rome. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Verona. To the Directory: I have caused these letters to be printed in the Bologna gazettes, so as to convince all Italy of the idiotic doting of these old cardinals.
voice: I have caused these letters to be printed in the Bologna gazettes, so as to convince all Italy of the idiotic doting of these old cardinals
tweet: Enclosed: intercepted letters proving Rome obstinacy — even Vienna refuses the Pope alliance, wanting peace. I print them in Bologna gazettes for all Italy to judge. Tomorrow I cross the Po at Ferrara, bound for Rome.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The words of peace which I charged you to convey to the Holy Father have been stifled by those men for whom the glory of Rome is nothing, but who are sold to the courts which employ them. We are drawing to the close of this ridiculous comedy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Verona. To Cardinal Mattel: The words of peace which I charged you to convey to the Holy Father have been stifled by those men for whom the glory of Rome is nothing…
voice: We are drawing to the close of this ridiculous comedy
tweet: Foreign intriguers ruin Rome; my words of peace are stifled by men sold to their employers. This comedy nears its end, but my letters prove their perfidy. Assure His Holiness he may rest in Rome without fear, under my protection.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Committee of Savants has reaped a good harvest at Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Ancona, Loretto, and Perugia which will be at once forwarded to Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Tolentino: the Pope pays for peace.
tweet: My savants reaped nobly at Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Ancona, Loretto, Perugia; all comes straight to Paris.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Joined to what is to be sent from Rome we now possess everything that is beautiful in Italy, with the exception of a small number of objects at Turin and Naples. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Tolentino. To the Directory: Joined to what is to be sent from Rome we now possess everything that is beautiful in Italy, with the exception of a small number of objects at Turin and Naples.
voice: Joined to what is to be sent from Rome we now possess everything that is beautiful in Italy, with the exception of a small number of objects at Turin and Naples
tweet: My savants have reaped Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Ancona, Loretto and Perugia — all forwarded to Paris at once. With what Rome must send, I now hold everything beautiful in Italy, save a few pieces at Turin and Naples.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: I brigadier rusca commands all romagna, spreading conquest further. The revolutionary flag advances.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Leclerc to Russi today, Ravenna on pacific signs. […]”

tweet: I Leclerc to russi today, Ravenna on pacific signs. The diplomatic advance continues.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

originalText: Ordre d'approvisionner Mantoue pour 12,000 hommes et 2,000 chevaux pendant un an, avec médicaments.
tweet: I Victual Mantua a yEAR for 12,000 men and 2,000 horse, drugs included. The fortress must hold.

tweet: I victor's vanguard to sinigaglia tomorrow. The offensive does not pause.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: I direct my Minister: Send Paris the Mantua flags Augereau took — they close the campaign. While Rome comes to reason, I prepare the next one.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: I Mantua ordinances: razings, congregations, gratifications. Order is imposed on the conquered city.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: Boudet shall bear the colours — the terrible regiment nothing can stop. Our enemies are driven into the snowy Noric Alps, cavalry charging over ice. But my Rhine armies must enter Germany.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

sourceTitle: To The General Administration Of Lombardy, Gratz, 1797-04-12

tweet: You ask guarantees for your independence — are my daily victories not assurances? Each one is a line in your charter. Facts replace declarations.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

voice: I have no intention of quitting the army After the signature of peace it is proposed that an expedition shall be undertaken against England or Portugal
tweet: Peace talks open within days — you cannot go to Paris before that, and I shall not quit the army. After the signature, England or Portugal: an expedition sails, and you shall choose which.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Enclosed Venice manifesto: print a thousand copies. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)

tweet: I Enclosed Venice manifesto: print a thousand copies. The proclamation must reach every citizen.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have sent to Toulon from Trieste 25,000 quintals of corn and 100,000 francs of hemp and steel. The Pope has given us eight millions in diamonds, which, according to valuation at Modena, are worth not more than 4,500,000 francs. […]”

tweet: I am organizing the Cisalpine Republic, and its millions march: one for Toulon tomorrow, another for Paris the day after, one for Brest — 7,000,000 francs in all, down to Corsica share.

tweet: Enclosed is Baraguey order. If you can get 3 or 4 millions, carry out the confiscation — gently, with least discontent to the Venetians. And squeeze Modena 6 millions, ready to seize on the inhabitants demand.

tweet: I am informed forty-five Vicentin parishes refuse their church plate. Take measures — make them furnish like the rest.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Transfer all Venetian soldier-prisoners to France. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter and prints received, Bishop; the motto displeased me. […]”

tweet: Your letter and prints received, Bishop; the motto displeased me. The Church must align with the Republic.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

originalText: Il y a eu des troubles en Corse, occasionnés par l'insurrection de la gendarmerie, qui n'était pas payée.
tweet: I Corsica troubles: unpaid gendarmerie risen. Order must be restored on the island.

tweet: You will find inclosed the ratification of the Emperor to the preliminary treaty. The plenipotentiary regretted the treaty not on parchment, seals not larger. I agree; parchment ought to be used for documents meant to be preserved.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

context: A general dictates peace to an emperor. To the Directory: If the Germanic Confederation did not exist it would be necessary to create it for our convenience.
tweet: I enclose the Emperor ratification — plenipotentiaries quibbling over parchment and seal sizes. Our plan tabled today: France to the Rhine, Salzburg and Passau to him, Cleves to Prussia, Venice to him, guarantees all round.

tweet: I have made young Eugène de Beauharnais sub-lieutenant of hussars and my aide-de-camp. Confirm it — he is a brave officer son, and the country will long mourn His Father.
